00

Before Day 1 · robotics primer

Inside a robot

What is a robot made of, and why does it need software like ROS 2?

About 40 minutes, before the ROS 2 overview. Every slide in this chapter is interactive: let participants call out which robot, part or setting to try next. Skip the anatomy and loop-rates slides if the room already builds robots.

Inside a robot · robot types

What is a robot?

Let the auto tour run through all six robots once, then click one the room cares about. Point out that the colours never change meaning: cyan senses, blue thinks, orange acts. Ask: what is the smallest robot in this room? (A phone with a vibration motor is arguably one.)

Inside a robot · the loop

Sense, think, act

Start at 0.2 s: the robot stops for the person and goes on. Then drag the thinking time towards 1.5 s and press new run: the robot now acts on a scan that is too old and drives into the person. Ask what makes thinking slow: heavy computation, a slow network, a busy computer. This is why loop rates and latency appear all through the workshop.

Inside a robot · TurtleBot3 Burger

Anatomy of a real robot

This is the robot we simulate on Day 2. Let the tour explode the stack and visit each part, then toggle URDF model to show the real mesh from turtlebot3_description. Map each part to sense, think or act. Specifications are from the ROBOTIS TurtleBot3 Burger specification; LDS-01 or LDS-02 depends on the kit year.

Inside a robot · sensors

Sensors: inside or outside?

Inside · proprioceptive

the robot measures itself

Outside · exteroceptive

the robot measures the world

Ask volunteers to drag cards. Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot itself; exteroceptive sensors measure the world. Every sensor reaches ROS 2 as a standard message type, shown on each card once it is sorted. Show answers fills the rest in one by one.

Inside a robot · actuators

Actuators need feedback

Open loop first: the wheel reaches the target until the ramp (pink band) adds load, then it slows and nothing corrects it. Switch to closed loop: the controller compares target and encoder and pushes harder. Then raise Kp above about 10: the 50 ms sensor delay makes it oscillate. ros2_control runs loops like this on every joint.

Inside a robot · autonomy

The autonomy stack

Let auto walk through the four stages for the mobile robot, then switch to the arm. Same four questions, different packages: Nav2 for mobile robots, MoveIt 2 for arms, ros2_control underneath both. We meet MoveIt 2 and ros2_control on Day 3.

Inside a robot · timing

Loops run at different speeds

Auto zoom sweeps from 10 ms to 10 s. At 10 ms only the motor loop ticks; at 10 s the motor, IMU, camera and controller lanes are solid. Rates are typical values: ros2_control at 1 kHz on the Panda, Nav2 controller_frequency 20 Hz, LDS-01 at 5 Hz, Nav2 replanning at 1 Hz. Different rates are one reason robots are split into many programs.

Inside a robot · the problem

Many programs, many computers

Follow /cmd_vel from the laptop to the motors, then /scan back. Three computers, three kinds of link, each with its own format. Drop Wi-Fi and ask what the robot should do. This is the problem ROS 2 solves between the Pi and the laptop: who is listening, what the data means, and how to deliver it. The next slide shows the same idea for any robot.

Inside a robot · why ROS 2

One robot, many programs

image / objectsaction goalmotor commands

ROS 2 gives these programs a shared way to discover, exchange typed data, and report state.

Let the first part play: six programs pairs, six different home-made links, each with its own format and failure modes. Then the links dissolve into one graph and the same data flows with standard tools to inspect it. Press K to pause on any hop. Begin with the software boundaries participants already understand, then introduce ROS names for the runtime pieces.

Inside a robot · check

Quick check

1. A TurtleBot3 decides from a lidar scan that is 1 s old while driving at 0.22 m/s. How far did it move without seeing?

Distance = speed × delay = 0.22 m/s × 1 s = 0.22 m. Slow thinking means driving blind.

2. Which of these sensors is proprioceptive (the robot measuring itself)?

Encoders measure the robot's own wheels. Lidar, camera and GPS measure the world outside.

3. Teleop on the laptop must reach the wheel motors through the Raspberry Pi. What does ROS 2 provide between the laptop and the Pi?

ROS 2 finds the other programs and delivers /cmd_vel as a typed message. The OpenCR firmware is below ROS.

Give pairs 30 seconds per question before anyone clicks. The score counts answers that were right the first time.

ROS

Before Day 1 · overview

What ROS 2 is and why it exists

Where did ROS come from, and what changed in ROS 2?

About 30 minutes. History and the ROS 1 comparison can be a pre-read if the room already knows ROS.

The ROS equation

What is ROS 2?

The stack builds itself: the operating system at the bottom (not ROS), then plumbing, tools, capabilities, and the community around everything. Click a layer or a button to stop and talk about it; the next four slides animate each term in detail. The point: participants reuse plumbing, tools, and capabilities so they can focus on their robot's unique problem.

ROS 2 equation · 1 of 4

Plumbing: how programs talk

message / requestresponse / resultfeedback

Discovery
nodes find each other

Interfaces
typed messages on the wire

QoS
delivery and history rules

Executors
run callbacks when data arrives

This one picture uses all three patterns from Day 1: topics for streams, a service for a quick question, and an action for a long task. Plumbing is everything that moves those messages.

ROS 2 equation · 2 of 4

Tools: see inside the system

The same tools work on every ROS 2 robot, because every robot speaks the same graph.

Each tool is just another node, or a client of the graph. That is why a tool written for one robot works on yours with no changes.

ROS 2 equation · 3 of 4

Capabilities: do not start from zero

Reuse tested packages for the common parts. Write only what makes your robot different.

Ask participants which block their own project lives in. Most real robots use several of these packages unchanged. Day 3 uses ros2_control and MoveIt 2 directly.

ROS 2 equation · 4 of 4

Community: you are not alone

Thousands of developers, companies, and universities maintain ROS 2 together, in the open.

Show participants how to search an error message on Robotics Stack Exchange and how to check that a package supports Jazzy on index.ros.org.

From a lab project to an industry standard

History of ROS and ROS 2

ROS 1 · 13 distributionsROS 2 · 12 distributions so far
Each letter is a distribution, named alphabetically. ROS 1 ran from Box Turtle to Noetic; ROS 2 restarted at A with Ardent. ROS 1 reached end of life on May 31, 2025. Pause with K to talk about any milestone.

docs.ros.org › Distributions

ROS 2 distributions over time

LTS · 5 yearsnon-LTS · about 1.5 yearsend of lifeRollingplanned
Releases are named alphabetically after turtles and arrive every May 23, World Turtle Day. Even years are LTS with five years of support; odd years get about 18 months. On the workshop date Humble, Jazzy, Kilted, and Lyrical are supported. Source: docs.ros.org Releases page.

Why a new version

Why ROS 2?

Four animated reasons, nine seconds each. 1: stop the ROS 1 master and the existing link keeps flowing, but the new /logger waits forever; in ROS 2 a node stops, the rest carry on, and /logger joins by discovery. 2: lifecycle states, SROS2 encryption, and Jazzy's five-year LTS. 3: on lossy Wi-Fi, reliable resends message 1 late while best effort skips it and stays fresh. 4: one graph across Linux, Windows, macOS and micro-ROS. ROS 1 was designed for research with one robot, a reliable network, and a single workstation; ROS 2 was redesigned rather than patched. ROS 1 reached end of life in May 2025.

Centralized vs distributed

ROS 1 vs ROS 2 architecture

registration / datamaster replyconnectfailed lookup
Let the left side reach step 4 and ask: what happens to a robot in the field if roscore crashes? Existing ROS 1 connections survive, but nothing new can start. ROS 2 has no roscore command at all.

Layer by layer

ROS 1 vs ROS 2 software stack

In ROS 1, roscpp and rospy were separate implementations, so features and bugs differed by language. In ROS 2, rcl is shared and rmw lets you swap the middleware without touching your code.

Side by side

ROS 1 vs ROS 2

ros1_bridge can connect ROS 1 and ROS 2 systems during migration, but ROS 1 is now end of life. Optional if time is short: summarize in two minutes and share the slide as a pre-read.

PRE

Before Day 1 · pre-read

Linux and Python essentials

What do you need before installing ROS 2 and writing your first node?

Share these slides before the workshop. Participants who already use the Linux terminal and Python classes daily can skip to the install check.

Linux terminal · 1 of 3

Navigate the file system

Press Tab to complete names. It saves typing and catches spelling mistakes in package and topic names too.

Every ROS workspace is a folder tree. Most beginner errors come from running a command in the wrong folder, so check pwd first.

Linux terminal · 2 of 3

Processes, search, and permissions

Never run colcon build or ros2 commands with sudo. Root-owned build files break later builds.

The pipe | sends one command's output into the next. It is the most useful idea on this slide: ros2 topic list | grep scan.

Linux terminal · 3 of 3

Environment and packages

# Install software from Ubuntu or ROS repositories
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-turtlesim

# Environment variables configure programs
echo $ROS_DISTRO
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7
printenv | grep ROS

# source runs a script in this terminal
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash

# ~/.bashrc runs in every new terminal
echo "export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7" >> ~/.bashrc

Why this matters for ROS 2

Use Ctrl+Shift+T for a new terminal tab and Ctrl+R to search command history.

Most "it works in one terminal but not another" problems are environment differences. Compare printenv | grep ROS in both terminals.

Self-check · 10 minutes

Self-check: Linux

  1. Create a workspace folder.
  2. Create and edit a file inside it.
  3. Find the file from your home folder.
  4. Set a variable and read it back.
  5. Open a new tab and check the variable again.

Done when you can explain why the variable is missing in the new tab.

mkdir -p ~/ros2_ws/src
cd ~/ros2_ws/src
nano hello.txt
cd ~
find ~/ros2_ws -name "hello.txt"

export ROBOT_NAME=turtle
echo $ROBOT_NAME

# New tab: Ctrl+Shift+T
echo $ROBOT_NAME
The empty result in the new tab is the same reason an unsourced terminal cannot find ros2.

Python · 1 of 3

Python basics

speed = 0.5                  # float
name = 'turtle1'             # string
joints = ['joint1', 'joint2'] # list
limits = {'max_speed': 1.0}  # dictionary

print(f'{name} moves at {speed} m/s')

for joint in joints:
    print(joint)

if speed > limits['max_speed']:
    print('too fast')
else:
    print('ok')

def clamp(value, low, high):
    return max(low, min(value, high))

Rules to remember

Run a file with python3 file.py. Try ideas in the python3 prompt.

ROS 2 Jazzy uses Python 3.12. Messages behave like objects with typed fields, and parameters often arrive as lists and dictionaries from YAML.

Python · 2 of 3

Classes and objects

class Robot:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name        # attribute
        self.speed = 0.0

    def drive(self, speed):    # method
        self.speed = speed
        print(f'{self.name}: {speed} m/s')

class Rover(Robot):            # inherits Robot
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('rover')

r = Rover()
r.drive(0.3)

Every ROS 2 node is a class

Your nodes write class Talker(Node) and call super().__init__('talker').

Spend the most time here. Participants who understand self and inheritance will read every rclpy example without trouble.

Python · 3 of 3

Imports and callbacks

import math
from std_msgs.msg import String   # from a package

def on_message(text):
    print('received:', text)

def subscribe(callback):
    # the caller decides what happens later
    for text in ['hello', 'world']:
        callback(text)

subscribe(on_message)   # pass the function, no ()

def main():
    print(math.pi)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

The callback idea

subscribe(on_message()) calls it immediately. Pass on_message without brackets.

This is the bridge to create_subscription(String, 'chatter', self.on_msg, 10) and create_timer(0.5, self.tick).

Self-check · 15 minutes

Self-check: Python

  1. Write a Robot class with a name and a battery level.
  2. Add a drive method that uses 10% battery.
  3. Refuse to drive below 20% battery.
  4. Call a callback each time the battery changes.

Done when the program prints each battery change through your callback.

class Robot:
    def __init__(self, name, on_change):
        self.name = name
        self.battery = 100
        self.on_change = on_change

    def drive(self):
        if self.battery <= 20:
            print('battery low')
            return
        self.battery -= 10
        self.on_change(self.battery)

r = Robot('rover', lambda b: print(f'battery {b}%'))
for _ in range(10):
    r.drive()
If this exercise feels easy, the Python in the workshop will too. If not, pair the participant with someone confident before Day 1.

SET

Before Day 1 · install check

Install and set up ROS 2

Is every laptop ready for the first lab?

Run this as a pre-workshop session or the first 30 minutes of Day 1. Pair anyone with problems with a working laptop rather than debugging live.

Setup · Ubuntu 24.04

Install ROS 2 Jazzy

  1. Set a UTF-8 locale.
  2. Enable the Ubuntu universe repository.
  3. Add the ROS 2 apt source.
  4. Install the desktop and developer tools.
  5. Source the setup file in every terminal.
# 1-2. Locale and universe
sudo apt update && sudo apt install locales software-properties-common curl
sudo locale-gen en_US en_US.UTF-8
sudo update-locale LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 LANG=en_US.UTF-8
sudo add-apt-repository universe

# 3. ROS 2 apt source
export ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/latest | grep -F "tag_name" | awk -F\" '{print $4}')
curl -L -o /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb "https://github.com/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/download/${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}/ros2-apt-source_${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}.$(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)_all.deb"
sudo dpkg -i /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb

# 4. Install
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop ros-dev-tools
Follow docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/Installation/Ubuntu-Install-Debs.html if anything differs. ros-jazzy-desktop includes RViz and demos; ros-jazzy-ros-base is the smaller option for robots without a screen. Docs: Installation › Ubuntu (deb packages).

Setup · Ubuntu 26.04 · newest LTS

Install ROS 2 Lyrical

  1. Use Ubuntu 26.04 (Resolute Raccoon).
  2. Repeat the locale, universe, and apt source steps.
  3. Install ros-lyrical-desktop.
  4. Source /opt/ros/lyrical/setup.bash.
# Same steps as Jazzy: the apt source package
# picks the Ubuntu codename (resolute) by itself
sudo apt update && sudo apt install locales software-properties-common curl
sudo add-apt-repository universe
export ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/latest | grep -F "tag_name" | awk -F\" '{print $4}')
curl -L -o /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb "https://github.com/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/download/${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}/ros2-apt-source_${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}.$(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)_all.deb"
sudo dpkg -i /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb

# Install and source
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
sudo apt install ros-lyrical-desktop ros-dev-tools
source /opt/ros/lyrical/setup.bash
echo $ROS_DISTRO   # lyrical
Lyrical Luth was released in May 2026 and is supported until 2031. It needs Ubuntu 26.04: each ROS 2 release is built for one Ubuntu LTS, so Jazzy stays on 24.04. The workshop labs use Jazzy; the code also builds on Lyrical, but check that every package you need (MoveIt, ros2_control, ros_gz) is released for Lyrical on index.ros.org before switching. Docs: docs.ros.org/en/lyrical/Installation.

Why source?

Most "command not found" errors mean the terminal was not sourced.

The Lab baseline slide verifies the install with talker and listener. Do not source two distributions in the same terminal. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Configuring environment.

Docs · Configuring environment

Configure the ROS environment

printenv | grep -i ROS
# ROS_VERSION=2  ROS_DISTRO=jazzy  …

# Keep this pair's robots apart (0-101 is safe)
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7

# How far automatic discovery reaches
export ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE=LOCALHOST
# SUBNET (default) · LOCALHOST · OFF · SYSTEM_DEFAULT

# Reach one machine without multicast
export ROS_STATIC_PEERS=192.168.1.20

In a classroom

ROS_LOCALHOST_ONLY is deprecated in Jazzy. Use ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE.

Assign domain IDs on the whiteboard before the first lab; 25 laptops on one Wi-Fi in the same domain will all see each other's turtles. Domain IDs above 101 can collide with operating-system ports on Linux.

Before the first lab

Common setup problems

Most first-day problems are the environment, not the code. Check the terminal before the program.

The 'em' error is real: colcon picks up whichever python3 comes first on PATH, and conda's Python lacks the empy module ROS needs to generate interfaces.

01

Day 1 · 09:30-11:00

Fundamentals of ROS 2 architecture

How do independent programs discover and exchange data?

Begin the first 90-minute block. Use 35 minutes for concepts, 20 minutes for the graph demo, and 35 minutes for the hands-on task. Pacing: 9 slides in this block, 0 marked Optional, 1 lab. One robot, many programs now closes the Inside a robot chapter. Skip Optional slides first if time runs short.

Core abstraction

The ROS 2 mental model

Node runs one focused part of the system.

Graph is the live network of ROS entities.

Interface defines the data contract.

Stress that a node is a runtime participant, not necessarily one executable or one process. Composition can place multiple nodes in one process. Docs: Concepts › Basic › Nodes.

Docs · Understanding nodes

Understanding nodes

# Terminal 1 and terminal 2
ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node
ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key

ros2 node list
# /teleop_turtle  /turtlesim
ros2 node info /turtlesim

# Start a second turtlesim with a new name
ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node \
  --ros-args --remap __node:=my_turtle

Read the output

Open rqt → Plugins → Services → Service Caller to call a service from a GUI.

Drive the turtle with the arrow keys in the teleop terminal. Ask participants to find, in ros2 node info /turtlesim, which topic the teleop node publishes to.

rcl · rclcpp · rclpy

ROS 2 client libraries

rclcpp · C++
drivers, control loops, speed

rclpy · Python
tools, prototypes, scripts

rclc · C
microcontrollers with micro-ROS

Community
rclrs (Rust), rclnodejs (JS), and more

rclcpp and rclpy are the two officially supported libraries. Both are thin layers over the same C library, rcl, so behavior is consistent and a Python node talks to a C++ node with no extra work.

Data Distribution Service

What is DDS?

  • An open standard from the Object Management Group (OMG)
  • Data-centric publish-subscribe
  • Automatic discovery with no broker
  • Rich Quality of Service policies
  • Wire protocol: RTPS over UDP
  • Proven in defense, aerospace, and finance

ROS 2 did not invent a new transport. It reused an industrial standard and put the rmw layer in front of it.

Nodes discover peers automatically when their domain, network, and interface contracts match. DDS is the default middleware family, but ROS 2 exposes a middleware abstraction, so avoid treating DDS as the only possible implementation. Because rmw abstracts the vendor, the same node binary works with different DDS implementations. Interoperability between vendors works over RTPS, but mixing vendors in one system is not recommended. Docs: Concepts › Advanced › ROS 2 middleware implementations.

rmw implementations

Types of DDS

# Choose the middleware per terminal
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp
ros2 doctor --report | grep middleware
All nodes in a system should use the same RMW. Install alternatives with apt, for example ros-jazzy-rmw-cyclonedds-cpp. Zenoh became a Tier 1 option from Kilted Kaiju and suits Wi-Fi and cloud links. Docs: Concepts › Intermediate › Different ROS 2 middleware vendors.

Finding the right peer

Names, namespaces, and domains

export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7
ros2 node list
ros2 topic list
Use namespaces for multiple robots that should communicate. Use domain IDs when the graphs should not discover each other. Docs: Concepts › Intermediate › The ROS_DOMAIN_ID.

Communication policy

Quality of Service changes behavior

A publisher and subscriber must have compatible QoS policies to communicate.

Show a camera subscriber failing because it expects reliable data while the camera offers best effort. Then use ros2 topic info --verbose. Docs: Concepts › Intermediate › Quality of Service settings.

Why a visible topic can stay silent

QoS compatibility

ros2 topic info /scan --verbose
ros2 topic echo /scan --qos-reliability best_effort
Requested reliability cannot exceed what the publisher offers. Use the verbose topic view to compare both endpoints. Docs: Concepts › Intermediate › Quality of Service settings.

02

Day 1 · 11:15-12:45

Topics and message interfaces

How does a stream of typed data move through the graph?

Second block. Aim to produce and inspect messages before writing a small publisher or subscriber. Pacing: 15 slides in this block, 2 marked Optional, 1 lab. Skip Optional slides first if time runs short.

Asynchronous streams

Publish and subscribe

sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan message · 10 Hz

Publishers do not address subscribers directly. They write typed samples to a named topic.

Watch one square: it splits at the topic, so every subscriber receives its own copy. The publisher never waits for a reply. Emphasize one-to-many and many-to-many communication. The topic name and type form the primary contract, with QoS completing it. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Understanding topics.

One sample, end to end

A message journey

When data is missing, inspect the journey from left to right.

The moving dot represents a sample. Pause at each stage and name the evidence: driver log, message fields, topic endpoint, QoS match, subscriber callback.

Typed contracts

Message interfaces are inspectable

ros2 interface show geometry_msgs/msg/Twist

# Output structure
Vector3 linear
  float64 x
  float64 y
  float64 z
Vector3 angular
  float64 x
  float64 y
  float64 z

Use standard interfaces before creating a custom message.

Point out that semantic conventions live in documentation and field comments, not only in primitive types. Docs: Concepts › Basic › Interfaces.

Observe before coding

Topic command-line tools

Make command-line introspection the first diagnostic habit. It separates graph and configuration problems from application-code problems. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Understanding topics.

Turtlesim demo

Topics: drive and listen

Twist on /turtle1/cmd_vel · 1 HzPose on /turtle1/pose · about 60 Hz

Where ROS finds your package

Workspaces and overlays

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
cd ~/ros2_ws
colcon build --symlink-install
source install/setup.bash
ros2 pkg prefix demo_py

A successful build does not update an already-open terminal until you source the overlay.

This slide addresses the most common beginner problem: a package builds but ros2 cannot find the new executable or launch file. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: Client libraries › Creating a workspace.

ament_python package

Package anatomy

demo_py/
├── package.xml        # name and dependencies
├── setup.py           # install rules
├── setup.cfg
├── resource/demo_py
├── launch/demo.launch.py
└── demo_py/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── talker.py
    └── listener.py
data_files=[
    ...,
    ('share/' + package_name + '/launch', glob('launch/*.launch.py')),
],
entry_points={
    'console_scripts': [
        'talker = demo_py.talker:main',
        'listener = demo_py.listener:main',
        ...
    ],
},
entry_points turn a Python function into a ros2 run executable. Add exec_depend entries in package.xml for every imported ROS package. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: Client libraries › Creating a package.

One workspace for every lab

Install dependencies with rosdep

rclpy · talker.py

Your first publisher

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String

class Talker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('talker')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(
            String, 'chatter', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.tick)
        self.count = 0

    def tick(self):
        msg = String(data=f'Hello {self.count}')
        self.pub.publish(msg)
        self.count += 1

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(Talker())
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, rclpy.executors.ExternalShutdownException):
        pass

Read it top to bottom

Type this live rather than pasting. Point out that the topic name has no leading slash, so it is relative to the node namespace. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: Client libraries › Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (Python).

rclpy · listener.py

Your first subscriber

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String

class Listener(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('listener')
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(
            String, 'chatter', self.on_msg, 10)

    def on_msg(self, msg):
        self.get_logger().info(f'I heard: {msg.data}')

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(Listener())
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, rclpy.executors.ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
# after creating the package in the 15:15 lab
colcon build --symlink-install
source install/setup.bash
ros2 run demo_py talker
ros2 run demo_py listener
The callback runs only while the node spins. Ask what happens if the listener uses the topic name "/chatter2". Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: Client libraries › Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (Python).

Optional · Docs · Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (C++)

Your first publisher in C++

#include "rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp"
#include "std_msgs/msg/string.hpp"
using namespace std::chrono_literals;
class Talker : public rclcpp::Node {
public:
  Talker() : Node("talker") {
    pub_ = create_publisher<std_msgs::msg::String>("chatter", 10);
    timer_ = create_wall_timer(500ms, [this]() {
      std_msgs::msg::String msg;
      msg.data = "Hello " + std::to_string(count_++);
      pub_->publish(msg);
    });
  }
private:
  rclcpp::Publisher<std_msgs::msg::String>::SharedPtr pub_;
  rclcpp::TimerBase::SharedPtr timer_;
  size_t count_ = 0;
};
int main(int argc, char * argv[]) {
  rclcpp::init(argc, argv);
  rclcpp::spin(std::make_shared<Talker>());
  rclcpp::shutdown();
}

...

Your first subscriber in C++

#include "rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp"
#include "std_msgs/msg/string.hpp"

class Listener : public rclcpp::Node {
public:
  Listener() : Node("listener") {

Day 1 · 13:30-15:00

Services and actions

Which interaction fits a request, and which fits a goal?

Third block. Compare communication patterns with concrete timing and feedback needs. Pacing: 12 slides in this block, 3 marked Optional, 1 lab. Skip Optional slides first if time runs short.

Design choice

Choose the interaction pattern

Timing and ownership matter more than the size of the payload.

Ask participants to classify examples: emergency stop state, save map, dock robot, set LED color.

Three questions

Communication pattern checklist

The questions are a practical starting point, not a formal protocol rule. Discuss ownership and failure semantics for ambiguous cases.

Synchronous exchange

Service request and response

requestresponse
ros2 service type /spawn
ros2 interface show turtlesim/srv/Spawn
ros2 service call /spawn turtlesim/srv/Spawn \
  "{x: 2.0, y: 3.0, theta: 0.0, name: 'turtle2'}"
Let the animation run twice: each client gets only its own response, and the server handles one request at a time. A service call may still be asynchronous in client code. The interaction semantics remain one request and one response. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Understanding services.

Turtlesim demo

Services: ask once, get one answer

requestresponse
Each call blocks the terminal until the single response arrives. The pen draws the teleport because turtle1's pen is down; ask how participants would turn it off (hint: the /turtle1/set_pen service). Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Understanding services.

Docs · Writing a simple service and client (Python)

Write a service server

from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

class MinimalService(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('minimal_service')
        self.srv = self.create_service(
            AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints', self.add)

    def add(self, request, response):
        response.sum = request.a + request.b
        self.get_logger().info(
            f'a: {request.a} b: {request.b}')
        return response

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(MinimalService())
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, rclpy.executors.ExternalShutdownException):
        pass

The server callback

ros2 service call /add_two_ints \
  example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts \
  "{a: 2, b: 3}"
# response: sum=5
Save it as demo_py/add_two_ints_server.py and add an entry point in setup.py. Test the server from the CLI before writing a client. Point out that the callback must return the response object.

Docs · Writing a simple service and client (Python)

Write a service client

class MinimalClientAsync(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('minimal_client_async')
        self.cli = self.create_client(AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints')
        while not self.cli.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0):
            self.get_logger().info('waiting for service...')

    def send_request(self, a, b):
        req = AddTwoInts.Request(a=a, b=b)
        return self.cli.call_async(req)

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    client = MinimalClientAsync()
    future = client.send_request(2, 3)
    rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(client, future)
    client.get_logger().info(f'sum: {future.result().sum}')
    client.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()

Asynchronous by design

Never block on a service call inside another callback: in a single-threaded executor the response can never be processed.

The future pattern is the same idea as the action client later in this block. Run server and client in two terminals and show what happens when the client starts first.

Long-running goals

Action lifecycle

requestresponsefeedback message
ros2 action info /turtle1/rotate_absolute
ros2 action send_goal --feedback /turtle1/rotate_absolute \
  turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute "{theta: 1.57}"
An action is built from two services and a topic. The client asks for the result early and waits while feedback streams back. Contrast cancellation with process termination. Cancellation is part of the application contract and can leave the robot in a safe state. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Understanding actions.

Turtlesim demo

Actions: a goal with progress

goal / result requestaccepted / resultfeedback
Turtlesim rotates at a fixed speed, so the feedback counts down. Press Ctrl+C during a second goal to show cancellation; the turtle stops where it is. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Understanding actions.

Optional · Docs · Creating an action

Create an action interface

int32 order                 # goal
---
int32[] sequence            # result
---
int32[] partial_sequence    # feedback

Three parts, one file

rosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME}
  "msg/Num.msg" "srv/AddThreeInts.srv"
  "action/Fibonacci.action")
Rebuild demo_interfaces, then check with ros2 interface show demo_interfaces/action/Fibonacci. Map each section to the action animation: goal service, result service, feedback topic. The three dashes separate the sections, exactly like the request and response of a .srv file.

Optional · Docs · Writing an action server and client (Python)

Write an action server

import time
from demo_interfaces.action import Fibonacci
from rclpy.action import ActionServer, CancelResponse

class FibonacciActionServer(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('fibonacci_action_server')
        self._server = ActionServer(
            self, Fibonacci, 'fibonacci', self.execute,
            cancel_callback=lambda goal: CancelResponse.ACCEPT)

    def execute(self, goal_handle):
        fb = Fibonacci.Feedback(partial_sequence=[0, 1])
        for i in range(1, goal_handle.request.order):
            if goal_handle.is_cancel_requested:
                goal_handle.canceled()
                return Fibonacci.Result(sequence=fb.partial_sequence)
            fb.partial_sequence.append(
                fb.partial_sequence[i] + fb.partial_sequence[i - 1])
            goal_handle.publish_feedback(fb)
            time.sleep(1)
        goal_handle.succeed()
        return Fibonacci.Result(sequence=fb.partial_sequence)

Long work, with progress

ros2 action send_goal --feedback \
  fibonacci \
  demo_interfaces/action/Fibonacci \
  "{order: 5}"
time.sleep stands in for real work such as moving an arm. Without goal_handle.succeed() the goal ends as aborted, which the CLI reports.

Optional · Docs · Writing an action server and client (Python)

Write an action client

from rclpy.action import ActionClient
class FibonacciActionClient(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('fibonacci_action_client')
        self._client = ActionClient(self, Fibonacci, 'fibonacci')

    def send_goal(self, order):
        self._client.wait_for_server()
        future = self._client.send_goal_async(
            Fibonacci.Goal(order=order),
            feedback_callback=self.on_feedback)
        future.add_done_callback(self.on_goal_response)

    def on_feedback(self, msg):
        self.get_logger().info(f'{list(msg.feedback.partial_sequence)}')

    def on_goal_response(self, future):
        handle = future.result()
        if handle.accepted:
            handle.get_result_async().add_done_callback(self.on_result)

    def on_result(self, future):
        result = future.result().result
        self.get_logger().info(f'result: {list(result.sequence)}')
        rclpy.shutdown()   # done: rclpy.spin() returns

Callbacks at each step

main() calls send_goal(10) and then rclpy.spin(client) so the callbacks can run.

Every arrow in the action animation is one of these calls. Cancellation uses handle.cancel_goal_async(); try it as an extension.

Day 1 · 15:15-16:45

Parameters, timers, and launch

How do we configure and start a repeatable robot system?

Final day-one block. Move from one-off commands to reproducible startup and runtime configuration. Pacing: 14 slides in this block, 4 marked Optional, 1 lab. Skip Optional slides first if time runs short.

Runtime configuration

Parameters configure nodes

ros2 param list /turtlesim
ros2 param describe /turtlesim background_r
ros2 param get /turtlesim background_r
ros2 param set /turtlesim background_r 20
ros2 param dump /turtlesim

Use parameters for configuration. Use topics for changing operational data.

Show that parameter behavior depends on node implementation. A set request may succeed only if the node declares and accepts the parameter. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Understanding parameters.

Turtlesim demo

Parameters: change behavior live

get / set requestresponse

Every node gets parameter services automatically: /turtlesim/get_parameters, /turtlesim/set_parameters, and more.

Run ros2 service list while turtlesim runs to show the parameter services. A node can reject a value in its parameter callback, and the CLI then prints the reason. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Understanding parameters.

Docs · Using parameters in a class (Python)

Use parameters in a node

from rcl_interfaces.msg import SetParametersResult

class MinimalParam(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('minimal_param_node')
        self.declare_parameter('my_parameter', 'world')
        self.add_on_set_parameters_callback(self.on_set)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.tick)

    def tick(self):
        name = self.get_parameter('my_parameter').value
        self.get_logger().info(f'Hello {name}!')

    def on_set(self, params):
        for p in params:
            if p.name == 'my_parameter' and not p.value:
                return SetParametersResult(
                    successful=False, reason='name is empty')
        return SetParametersResult(successful=True)

Declare, read, validate

ros2 run demo_py minimal_param_node \
  --ros-args -p my_parameter:=earth
ros2 param set /minimal_param_node my_parameter ""
# Setting parameter failed: name is empty
Undeclared parameters are rejected by default, which catches typos. Load many values at once with --ros-args --params-file params.yaml.

Periodic work

Timers schedule callbacks

class Heartbeat(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('heartbeat')
        self.timer = self.create_timer(
            0.5, self.on_timer)

    def on_timer(self):
        self.get_logger().info('alive')

Executor rule

A timer marks a callback ready. An executor decides when a thread runs it.

A long callback delays other work in a single-threaded executor.

A timer does not create a dedicated real-time thread. Use this distinction to explain jitter and callback groups later. Docs: Concepts › Intermediate › Executors.

Optional · Docs · Concepts: Executors

Executors and callback groups

from rclpy.callback_groups import MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup
from rclpy.executors import MultiThreadedExecutor
class Robot(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('robot')
        slow = MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup()   # one group per timer:
        fast = MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup()   # they may run at the same time
        self.create_timer(2.0, self.plan, callback_group=slow)
        self.create_timer(0.5, self.control, callback_group=fast)

    def plan(self):
        time.sleep(1.5)                  # slow work
        self.get_logger().info('plan ready')

    def control(self):
        self.get_logger().info('control tick')

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(Robot(), executor=MultiThreadedExecutor())
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, rclpy.executors.ExternalShutdownException):
        pass

Who runs your callbacks

With rclpy.spin, the 1.5 s plan freezes every control tick.

Run it twice: with rclpy.spin(Robot()) the control ticks stop during plan; with the multi-threaded executor they keep coming. Each timer gets its own group, so they can run at the same time.

Repeatable startup

Launch describes a system

  • Start multiple nodes
  • Apply parameters and remaps
  • Group nodes in namespaces
  • Include other launch files
  • React to startup events
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch_ros.actions import Node

def generate_launch_description():
    return LaunchDescription([
        Node(
            package='turtlesim',
            executable='turtlesim_node',
            namespace='demo',
            parameters=[{'background_r': 20}],
        )
    ])
Launch files are programs, but keep them declarative where possible. Separate configuration data into YAML when it improves reuse. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › Launch › Creating a launch file.

Turtlesim demo

Launch: one command, a whole system

cmd_velpose
This is the official 'Creating a launch file' tutorial. One launch file starts three nodes, namespaces keep the turtles apart, and remappings wire mimic between them without code changes. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › Launch › Creating a launch file.

3D · robot_state_publisher, joint_state_publisher, RViz

Launch a robot model

This launch file was run on Jazzy with the Panda URDF; the log lines are its real output. robot_state_publisher alone only publishes fixed transforms, so moving links have no TF until joint_state_publisher starts: at all-zero joints tf2_echo reports the hand at 0.088, 0.000, 0.926. Ctrl+C stops every node the file started. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › URDF › Using URDF with robot_state_publisher.

Optional · Docs · Launch: using substitutions

Launch arguments and substitutions

from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument
from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration
from launch_ros.actions import Node

def generate_launch_description():
    return LaunchDescription([
        DeclareLaunchArgument('ns', default_value='turtlesim1'),
        DeclareLaunchArgument('background_r', default_value='69'),
        Node(
            package='turtlesim', executable='turtlesim_node',
            namespace=LaunchConfiguration('ns'),
            parameters=[{
                'background_r': LaunchConfiguration('background_r')}]),
    ])

Values decided at launch time

ros2 launch demo_launch turtles.launch.py --show-args
ros2 launch demo_launch turtles.launch.py \
  ns:=robot1 background_r:=200
One launch file now starts any number of differently configured robots. --show-args prints every argument with its default, which documents the file for free.

Optional · Docs · Launch: using event handlers

Launch event handlers

from importlib.util import find_spec
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import (EmitEvent, ExecuteProcess, LogInfo,
                            RegisterEventHandler)
from launch.event_handlers import OnProcessExit, OnProcessStart
from launch.events import Shutdown
from launch_ros.actions import Node

MSGS = 'turtlesim_msgs' if find_spec('turtlesim_msgs') else 'turtlesim'

def generate_launch_description():
    sim = Node(package='turtlesim', executable='turtlesim_node')
    spawn = ExecuteProcess(cmd=[
        'ros2', 'service', 'call', '/spawn', f'{MSGS}/srv/Spawn',
        "{x: 2.0, y: 2.0, name: 'turtle2'}"])
    return LaunchDescription([
        sim,
        RegisterEventHandler(OnProcessStart(
            target_action=sim, on_start=[spawn])),
        RegisterEventHandler(OnProcessExit(
            target_action=sim,
            on_exit=[LogInfo(msg='turtlesim closed'),
                     EmitEvent(event=Shutdown())])),
    ])

React to what happens

Close the turtlesim window and the whole launch shuts down instead of leaving orphan nodes.

Event handlers turn a launch file from a list into a startup sequence. ros2 service call waits for /spawn to exist, so the spawn succeeds even if turtlesim takes a moment to start.

Optional · Docs · Launch: integrating launch files

Launch files in XML and YAML

<launch>
  <arg name="ns" default="turtlesim1"/>
  <node pkg="turtlesim" exec="turtlesim_node"
        namespace="$(var ns)">
    <param name="background_r" value="200"/>
  </node>
</launch>
launch:
- arg:
    name: ns
    default: turtlesim1
- node:
    pkg: turtlesim
    exec: turtlesim_node
    namespace: $(var ns)
    param:
    - name: background_r
      value: 200

# ros2 launch demo_launch turtles.launch.yaml ns:=robot1
Python, XML, and YAML launch files can include each other. Use Python when you need logic; XML or YAML for simple, readable setups. These two files start exactly the same node as the Python launch file on the "Launch arguments and substitutions" slide.

ros2 bag and rqt

Record, replay, and visualize

A bag lets you debug a robot run at your desk, again and again, without the robot.

Jazzy records bags in MCAP format by default. Record turtlesim while driving it, stop the teleop, then replay the bag and watch the turtle repeat the motion. Docs: Tutorials › Beginner: CLI tools › Recording and playing back data.

Turtlesim demo

Day 2 · 09:30-11:00

TF2 and coordinate systems

Where is an observation, and when was it true?

First day-two block. Establish frame semantics before tools and code.

Spatial relationships

A tree of coordinate frames

Frame names a coordinate system.

Transform stores translation, rotation, and time.

Tree gives one parent to each child frame.

Use the convention that frame IDs omit a leading slash. Explain map to odom and odom to base_link as separate responsibilities. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › tf2 › Introducing tf2.

3D · TurtleBot3 · map, odom, base_link

Frames move with the robot

TurtleBot3 Burger from turtlebot3_description. The odometry error (4% speed, small yaw-rate bias) is exaggerated so drift shows within a minute. Turn localization off: map → odom stays identity and the robot follows the drifting odometry. Drag to orbit. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › tf2.

3D · lookup_transform between any two frames

TF tree explorer

The tree: world has two children, the Panda (panda_link0 down to panda_hand) and a fixed camera_link that detects a cup. To grasp, the robot needs the cup in panda_hand: tf2 chains hand → … → world → camera_link → cup, the orange line. tf2 walks up from both frames to their common parent and multiplies every transform on the way. Pick any pair with the selectors; tour cycles through useful lookups. Compare with ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo target source.

Right-handed frames

Coordinate axes and rotation

+x
forward

+y
left

+z
up

Rotation
right-hand rule

Always confirm the convention used by the specific sensor or robot package.

ROS body frames commonly use x forward, y left, z up. Optical camera frames use a different convention, so verify the documented frame.

3D · roll, pitch, yaw

Rotations and quaternions

Angles follow tf2 setRPY: R = Rz(yaw) · Ry(pitch) · Rx(roll). Copy the command from the panel into a terminal and compare with ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo parent child. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › tf2 › Quaternion fundamentals.

Geometry with time

Transform a stamped observation

ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo \
  base_link camera_link

ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames

ros2 topic echo /tf_static \
  --qos-durability transient_local
Time is part of the transform query. A correct spatial chain with stale timestamps can still cause extrapolation errors.

Publisher ownership

Static and dynamic transforms

A child frame must have one authoritative parent publisher.

Duplicate publishers can produce jumps that look like sensor or localization noise. Use tf2_monitor and node introspection to find ownership. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › tf2.

Optional · Docs · tf2: writing a static broadcaster

Publish a static transform

# From the command line
ros2 run tf2_ros static_transform_publisher \
  --x 0.1 --y 0.0 --z 0.2 \
  --roll 0 --pitch 0 --yaw 0 \
  --frame-id base_link --child-frame-id lidar_link

ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo base_link lidar_link

Or from a node

from geometry_msgs.msg import TransformStamped
from tf2_ros.static_transform_broadcaster import (
    StaticTransformBroadcaster)

t = TransformStamped()
t.header.stamp = self.get_clock().now().to_msg()
t.header.frame_id = 'base_link'
t.child_frame_id = 'lidar_link'
t.transform.translation.x = 0.1
t.transform.translation.z = 0.2
t.transform.rotation.w = 1.0
self.tf_static = StaticTransformBroadcaster(self)
self.tf_static.sendTransform(t)
Static transforms are published once on /tf_static with transient-local durability, so late subscribers still receive them. Rotation w = 1.0 means no rotation. On a real robot, robot_state_publisher sends these from the URDF fixed joints.

Optional · Docs · tf2: writing a broadcaster (Python)

Write a tf2 broadcaster

import math
from geometry_msgs.msg import TransformStamped
from tf2_ros import TransformBroadcaster
from turtlesim.msg import Pose

class FramePublisher(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('turtle_tf2_frame_publisher')
        self.turtlename = self.declare_parameter('turtlename', 'turtle1').value
        self.br = TransformBroadcaster(self)
        self.create_subscription(
            Pose, f'/{self.turtlename}/pose', self.on_pose, 1)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        t = TransformStamped()
        t.header.stamp = self.get_clock().now().to_msg()
        t.header.frame_id = 'world'
        t.child_frame_id = self.turtlename
        t.transform.translation.x = msg.x
        t.transform.translation.y = msg.y
        t.transform.rotation.z = math.sin(msg.theta / 2)
        t.transform.rotation.w = math.cos(msg.theta / 2)
        self.br.sendTransform(t)

Pose in, transform out

ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node
ros2 run demo_tf2 turtle_frame_publisher
ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key
ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo world turtle1
Drive the turtle with teleop and watch tf2_echo update. The same pattern turns odometry into odom → base_link on a real robot.

Optional · Docs · tf2: writing a listener (Python)

Write a tf2 listener

from rclpy.time import Time
from tf2_ros import TransformException
from tf2_ros.buffer import Buffer
from tf2_ros.transform_listener import TransformListener

class FrameListener(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('frame_listener')
        self.target = self.declare_parameter('target', 'world').value
        self.source = self.declare_parameter('source', 'turtle1').value
        self.buffer = Buffer()
        self.listener = TransformListener(self.buffer, self)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.on_timer)

    def on_timer(self):
        try:
            t = self.buffer.lookup_transform(self.target, self.source, Time())
        except TransformException as ex:
            self.get_logger().info(f'not yet: {ex}')
            return
        p = t.transform.translation
        self.get_logger().info(f'{self.source} at x={p.x:.2f} y={p.y:.2f}')

Ask, do not track

The first lookups fail until the buffer has data: always catch TransformException.

Run the broadcaster, teleop, and this listener together. Then stop the broadcaster and show the exception message, which names the missing frame.

Day 2 · 11:15-12:45

URDF robot modeling

How does a robot description connect shape, motion, and frames?

Second day-two block. Build a small model incrementally and visualize after each joint.

Robot description

Links and joints form a kinematic tree

Link carries visual, collision, and inertial properties.

Joint connects parent and child links with motion limits.

Origin positions geometry and joint frames.

joint1 swings within its ±0.61 rad limit from the URDF on the right; joint2 moves link_2 and tool0 with it because they are children. URDF represents a tree, not a general closed-loop mechanism. More advanced constraints need additional modeling strategies. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › URDF › Building a visual robot model from scratch.

Geometry roles

One link, three models

A beautiful mesh does not guarantee a stable simulation.

Show that visual and collision origins can differ, but unexplained differences are a common source of confusion.

3D · Franka Panda URDF

Build the robot in 3D

Model: moveit_resources_panda_description, the URDF MoveIt uses on Day 3. Orange arrows are joint axes from the URDF; collision meshes are the simplified STL files. Point out the missing inertial tags. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › URDF.

Reusable descriptions

Xacro removes repetition

<xacro:macro name="wheel" params="name y">
  <link name="${name}">
    ...
  </link>
  <joint name="${name}_joint" type="continuous">
    <origin xyz="0 ${y} 0"/>
    <parent link="base_link"/>
    <child link="${name}"/>
    ...
  </joint>
</xacro:macro>

Validate early

check_urdf /tmp/robot.urdf
urdf_to_graphiz /tmp/robot.urdf
Newer urdfdom renames urdf_to_graphiz to urdf_to_graphviz.
Xacro expands to URDF. Debug the expanded file when macro errors obscure the final structure. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › URDF › Using Xacro to clean up your code.

robot_state_publisher

From URDF to TF

ros2 run robot_state_publisher robot_state_publisher \

ros2 run joint_state_publisher_gui joint_state_publisher_gui
Fixed joints go to /tf_static once. Moving joints need /joint_states; without it RViz shows those links with "No transform" errors. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › URDF › Using URDF with robot_state_publisher.

See what ROS sees

RViz2 tour

SymptomLikely causeCheck
No transformFrame missing from the TF treetf2_echo, view_frames
Nothing visibleWrong fixed frameSet it to base_link or map
Empty scanQoS mismatchSet reliability to Best Effort
RViz is a visualizer, not a simulator. It only draws what is published. Save the config with File > Save Config As and load it from launch with -d. Docs: Tutorials › Intermediate › RViz › RViz User Guide.

A stable modeling sequence

URDF build order

Validate in RViz after each stage. A small error stays easy to locate.

This order separates structural errors from mesh and simulation errors. Encourage frequent check_urdf runs.

Day 2 · 13:30-15:00

Gazebo simulation

How do model, physics, and ROS interfaces meet?

Third day-two block. The baseline pairs ROS 2 Jazzy with Gazebo Harmonic. Docs: Tutorials › Advanced › Simulators › Gazebo.

Digital experiment

Simulation loop

Simulation advances in discrete time. Real-time factor reports how quickly those steps run.

Each lap of the dot is one physics step; Gazebo's default step is 1 ms, so /clock advances 0.001 s per lap. Differentiate simulation time from wall time. Nodes using use_sim_time follow the /clock topic.

3D · /clock and use_sim_time

Simulation time in practice

Gazebo publishes /clock; nodes started with use_sim_time:=true read time from it. Pause the simulation: the sim-time timer stops while the wall-clock timer keeps ticking. A real-time factor below 1 means the computer cannot keep up.

Model boundaries

URDF, SDF, and the ROS bridge

URDF robot kinematic description used throughout ROS.

SDF simulation description for worlds, models, sensors, and plugins.

ros_gz_bridge converts each topic between the two message systems.

Avoid implying that all Gazebo interfaces appear in ROS automatically. Bridge only the data the application needs.

First run

Simulation startup checklist

Check one layer at a time before launching the full application.

Use this checklist during the lab. It keeps model, bridge, and controller problems separate.

Physics quality

Stable simulation starts with the model

Tune only after units, mass, inertia, and collision geometry are credible.

Show one deliberately bad inertia value if time permits. Participants remember the failure mode better than a formula alone.

Day 2 · 15:15-16:45

Sensor simulation

What makes simulated data useful for real software?

Final day-two block. Focus on data contracts, frames, rate, noise, and validation.

Data contract

A sensor is more than geometry

A sensor pipeline is valid only when data, frame, timestamp, and units agree.

Use this checklist whenever a point cloud or scan looks wrong. Visualization alone cannot prove timestamps and units are correct.

Gazebo Harmonic

Common simulated sensors

Message names shown are typical ROS-facing interfaces. Gazebo transport types differ before bridging.

From array index to direction

Reading a LaserScan message

angle_mindirection of the first sample

angle_incrementangle between samples

ranges[i]distance for sample i

range_min / range_maxvalid sensor limits

angle_i = angle_min + i * angle_increment
distance_i = ranges[i]
Invalid readings may appear as infinity or NaN. Check the message definition and sensor documentation before filtering.

3D · TurtleBot3 LDS-01

A lidar in a room

The scan uses the TurtleBot3 LDS-01 settings: 360 samples 1° apart, 0.12 to 3.5 m. Out-of-range readings become inf, as in a real LaserScan. Add noise to show why filtering matters; switch on the camera frustum and IMU arrows to compare sensors.

Evidence before algorithms

Day 3 · 09:30-11:00

Fundamentals of manipulators

How do joint values determine an end-effector pose?

First day-three block. Use a simple two-link arm before the six-axis example.

Two views of motion

Configuration and task space

Inverse kinematics searches in the opposite direction and may find zero, one, or many solutions.
Discuss why a pose can have multiple elbow configurations and why joint limits remove some solutions.

3D · forward kinematics

Joint space and task space in 3D

At the home pose the readout shows the hand at x 0.307, z 0.590: the same value tf2 gives from robot_state_publisher with this URDF. Sample the workspace: the cloud is every hand position from random joint values, coloured by height.

Joints ⇄ tool pose

Forward and inverse kinematics

# Two-link planar arm, link lengths l1 and l2
x = l1·cos(q1) + l2·cos(q1 + q2)
y = l1·sin(q1) + l2·sin(q1 + q2)
Draw the elbow-up and elbow-down solutions for one target point. An unreachable target has no IK solution; near a singularity, small tool motions need very large joint motions.

3D · numeric IK

Inverse kinematics in 3D

A numeric solver like KDL: it repeatedly moves the joints along the Jacobian toward the target. The target passes out of reach on purpose. Other solution re-solves from a different starting guess: same hand pose, different arm shape.

What the robot can reach

Degrees of freedom and workspace

Reachability depends on

  • Joint types and limits
  • Link lengths and offsets
  • Required tool orientation
  • Self-collision and obstacles

Inside the geometric reach does not always mean collision-free or controllable.

Near singularities, small Cartesian motion can require large joint motion. Use an extended-arm example.

From intent to motors

The manipulation stack

Planning decides where to move. Control drives the robot along the chosen trajectory.

This distinction prepares participants for MoveIt 2 versus ros2_control responsibilities.

Day 3 · 11:15-12:45

ros2_control and MoveIt 2 architecture

How does a planned trajectory reach simulated or real hardware?

Second day-three block. Show responsibilities first, then configuration files and controller lifecycle.

Hardware abstraction

ros2_control closes the loop

State interfaces flow up. Command interfaces flow down.

Controller Manager matches controller claims to hardware interfaces and runs the update loop.

3D · command vs state

ros2_control tracking loop

The ghost arm is the command interface, the solid arm the state interface. The joints are simulated as a PD loop; raise Kp to cut the lag, lower damping to see overshoot. Real controllers run this read, update, write loop at the controller_manager update_rate.

Planning architecture

MoveIt 2 planning components

The planning scene combines the robot state, attached objects, and world collision geometry.

MoveIt 2 does not replace a trajectory controller. It produces and monitors trajectories that a controller executes.

What the planner believes

The planning scene

A planner can avoid only the objects represented in its planning scene.

Compare the Gazebo world and the MoveIt planning scene. They are separate representations and must be synchronized by the application.

Runtime ownership

Controller lifecycle

ros2 control list_hardware_interfaces
ros2 control list_controllers
ros2 control load_controller --set-state active joint_state_broadcaster
ros2 control load_controller --set-state inactive arm_controller
ros2 control switch_controllers --activate arm_controller

Two active controllers cannot claim the same command interface.

Inspect claimed interfaces when a controller fails to activate. The error often identifies a name mismatch or ownership conflict.

Day 3 · 13:30-15:00

Fundamentals of motion planning

How does a robot search for a valid path through configuration space?

Third day-three block. Keep the mathematics conceptual and connect each term to visible MoveIt behavior.

Search problem

Planning in configuration space

State is a vector of joint values.

Validity checks limits and collisions.

Path connects valid states continuously.

Obstacles in workspace become forbidden regions in configuration space, often with complex shapes.

Canvas · sampling-based planning

RRT-Connect in configuration space

RRT-Connect is the default OMPL planner in MoveIt. A two-link arm keeps configuration space 2D so it can be drawn; the Panda has 7 dimensions, which is why planners sample instead of mapping it.

Executable motion

From path to trajectory

A geometric path becomes a trajectory only after time and dynamic limits are added.

Explain why a plan can be collision-free yet too aggressive for the physical robot if limits are wrong.

3D · velocity and acceleration

Time parameterization

MoveIt adds timing with a time-parameterization adapter. Path only moves at constant speed and stops dead at each waypoint, which needs infinite acceleration. Compare the peak values between modes.

What defines an acceptable solution

Planning request constraints

A narrow orientation tolerance can make an otherwise reachable goal difficult to plan.

Change one constraint at a time during troubleshooting. Preserve collision checking rather than disabling safety checks.

Structured diagnosis

Planning failures are evidence

Read the MoveIt logs and error code before changing random parameters. Reproduce with the smallest planning scene.

Day 3 · 15:15-16:45

Cartesian motion and grasping

How do we turn a tool path into a complete manipulation task?

Final scheduled block. Connect straight-line tool motion to approach, grasp, lift, and retreat.

Path semantics

Joint motion and Cartesian motion

Straight tool motion can approach a singularity or joint limit.

Cartesian interpolation is local. It does not remove the need for collision checking, jump thresholds, or path fraction validation.

3D · two Pandas, same start and goal

Joint vs Cartesian motion in 3D

The Cartesian arm follows a straight line by solving IK at 80 points along it, the idea behind computeCartesianPath. Fraction 1.00 means every point was solved; a lower fraction means the line is only partly reachable.

Manipulation task

A grasp is a sequence

The planning scene must reflect the object attachment after grasp. Otherwise the held object may be ignored during collision checking.

3D · attach and detach

Pick and place in 3D

Every pose comes from the IK solver at load time. The box turns orange while it is attached to panda_hand in the planning scene and green when it is a world object again.

Planning scene updates

Object state during pick and place

Attach after closing the gripper. Detach only after the object reaches its supported placement.

The physical gripper and the planning scene must change consistently. Otherwise the plan can collide with the held object or forget it entirely.

Candidate evaluation

Grasp feasibility filters

A good grasp must work as a motion sequence, not only as a final hand pose.

MoveIt Task Constructor is well suited to staged manipulation pipelines. Keep the introduction conceptual in Phase I.

Composition: many nodes, one process

Why compose

In launch files, use ComposableNodeContainer with ComposableNode entries.

Managed lifecycle nodes

ros2 run lifecycle lifecycle_talker
ros2 run lifecycle lifecycle_listener

ros2 lifecycle nodes

A node with a startup contract

Docs · Testing

Test your packages

# demo_py/test/test_clamp.py
# clamp() lives in demo_py/util.py
from demo_py.util import clamp


def test_clamp_limits():
    assert clamp(5, 0, 1) == 1
    assert clamp(-1, 0, 1) == 0
    assert clamp(0.5, 0, 1) == 0.5

# From the workspace root
colcon test --packages-select demo_py
colcon test-result --verbose

What runs

Keep logic in plain functions so it can be tested without starting ROS.

colcon test does not stop on failure; colcon test-result shows which tests failed and why. Fix the style warnings early, they pile up quickly.

ROS 2 security with SROS2

ros2 security create_enclave demo_keystore /talker_listener/talker
ros2 security create_enclave demo_keystore /talker_listener/listener

export ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE=$PWD/demo_keystore
export ROS_SECURITY_ENABLE=true
export ROS_SECURITY_STRATEGY=Enforce

ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker \
  --ros-args --enclave /talker_listener/talker
ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener \
  --ros-args --enclave /talker_listener/listener

DDS-Security, switched on

With Enforce, a node without valid keys cannot join the graph at all.

Show tcpdump or Wireshark before and after: with security on, the payload is unreadable. Each enclave is a folder of certificates; keep the keystore's private keys out of version control.
